title: Book 2, Chapter 8 — Third Year of the War—Investment of Plataea—Naval Victories of Phormio—Thracian Irruption into Macedonia under Sitalces
paragraphs: The next summer the Peloponnesians and their allies, instead of invading Attica, marched against Plataea under the command of Archidamus, son of Zeuxidamus, king of the Lacedaemonians. He had already encamped his army and was about to lay waste the country when the Plataeans hurried to send envoys to him, who spoke as follows: “Archidamus and Lacedaemonians, in invading Plataean territory you do what is wrong in itself, and unworthy of yourselves and of the fathers who begot you. Pausanias, son of Cleombrotus, your countryman, after freeing Hellas from the Medes with the help of those Hellenes who were willing to share the risk of the battle fought near our city, sacrificed to Zeus the Liberator in the marketplace of Plataea. Calling all the allies together, he restored to the Plataeans their city and territory and declared it independent and inviolate against aggression or conquest. Should any such attempt be made, the allies present were to defend us with all their might. Your fathers rewarded us in this way for the courage and patriotism we showed at that perilous time. Yet you do the very opposite, coming with our bitterest enemies, the Thebans, to enslave us. We appeal, therefore, to the gods to whom those oaths were sworn, to the gods of your ancestors, and finally to the gods of our own country, and we call on you to refrain from violating our territory or breaking those oaths, and to leave us to live independent, as Pausanias decreed.”

The Plataeans had got this far when they were cut short by Archidamus, who said: “There is justice, Plataeans, in what you say, if you act on your words. By the grant of Pausanias, you yourselves should remain independent — and you should join in freeing those of your fellow countrymen who, after sharing the dangers of that period, joined in the oaths to you, and who are now subject to the Athenians. It is to free them and the rest that all this preparation and war has been undertaken. I would prefer that you share our labours and abide by the oaths yourselves; but if that is impossible, then do what we have already asked of you — remain neutral, enjoy what is your own, join neither side, and receive both as friends, neither as allies for the war. With that we shall be satisfied.” Such were the words of Archidamus. After hearing what he had to say, the Plataeans went into the city and reported it to the people, and presently came back with the answer that it was impossible for them to do as he proposed without consulting the Athenians, with whom their wives and children now were. Besides, they had their fears for the town. After his departure, what was to stop the Athenians from coming and taking it out of their hands, or the Thebans, who would be included in the oaths, from exploiting the proposed neutrality to make a second attempt to seize the city? On these points he tried to reassure them by saying: “You have only to hand over the city and houses to us Lacedaemonians, to point out the boundaries of your land, the number of your fruit-trees, and whatever else can be counted, and to withdraw yourselves wherever you like for the duration of the war. When it is over we will give back to you whatever we received, and in the meantime hold it in trust and keep it under cultivation, paying you a sufficient allowance.”

When they had heard this, they re-entered the city, consulted with the people, and said that they wished first to inform the Athenians of the proposal, and to accept it if Athens approved. In the meantime they asked him to grant a truce and not to lay waste their territory. He accordingly granted a truce for the number of days needed for the journey, and meanwhile refrained from ravaging their land. The Plataean envoys went to Athens, conferred with the Athenians, and came back with this message for those in the city: “The Athenians say, Plataeans, that since you became their allies they have never on any occasion abandoned you to an enemy, and they will not neglect you now, but will help you to the best of their ability. They charge you, by the oaths your fathers swore, to keep the alliance unaltered.”

When the envoys delivered this message, the Plataeans resolved not to be unfaithful to the Athenians, and to endure, if it must be, the sight of their lands laid waste and any other trials that came their way. They would not send out again, but would answer from the wall that it was impossible for them to do as the Lacedaemonians proposed. As soon as he had received this reply, King Archidamus first made a solemn appeal to the gods and heroes of the country, in these words: “You gods and heroes of the Plataean territory, be my witnesses that we did not invade this land as aggressors from the start, nor until these people had first abandoned the common oath. This is the land where our fathers offered you their prayers before defeating the Medes, and which you made auspicious to Hellenic arms. Nor shall we be aggressors in the measures we now take, since we have made many fair proposals and have not succeeded. Grant graciously that those who were the first to offend may be punished for it, and that those who would justly take vengeance may obtain it.”

After this appeal to the gods, Archidamus put his army in motion. First he enclosed the town with a palisade made of the fruit-trees they had cut down, to prevent any further movement out of Plataea. Next they raised a mound against the city, hoping that the size of the force employed would secure the rapid reduction of the place. They accordingly cut down timber from Cithaeron and built it up on either side, laying it lattice-fashion to serve as a frame to keep the mound from spreading, and carried up wood and stones and earth and any other material that would help complete it. They worked at the mound for seventy days and nights without a break, divided into relief parties so that some could be carrying while others slept and ate, the Lacedaemonian officer attached to each contingent keeping the men at the work. But the Plataeans, watching the mound rise, built a wooden wall and fixed it on that part of the city wall against which the mound was being raised, and filled in bricks inside it taken from the neighbouring houses. The timbers served to bind the structure together and to prevent it from weakening as it grew taller. It also had a covering of skins and hides, which protected the woodwork against burning missiles and allowed the men to work in safety. So the wall was raised to a great height, while the mound opposite made no less rapid progress. The Plataeans also thought of another expedient: they pulled out part of the wall against which the mound abutted and carried the earth into the city.

When the Peloponnesians discovered this, they twisted up clay in wattles of reed and threw it into the gap formed in the mound, to give it consistency and stop it from being carried away like the loose soil. Foiled in this, the Plataeans changed their method: they ran a tunnel from the town, calculated their way under the mound, and began to carry off its material as before. This went on for a long time without the enemy outside finding out, so that for all they threw on top, the mound made no proportional progress — it was being carried away from beneath and was constantly sinking down into the void. But the Plataeans, fearing that even so they might not be able to hold out against the superior numbers of the enemy, had yet another invention. They stopped working on the large structure in front of the mound, and starting at either end of it inside from the old low wall, built a new one in the shape of a crescent curving in toward the town. The idea was that if the great wall were taken, this one would remain, and the enemy would have to raise a fresh mound against it; and as they advanced within, they would not only have all their trouble to do over again, but would also be exposed to missiles on their flanks. While raising the mound, the Peloponnesians also brought up engines against the city. One of these was set on the mound against the large structure and shook down a good piece of it, to the no small alarm of the Plataeans. Others were brought up against different parts of the wall, but were lassoed and broken by the Plataeans, who also hung up great beams by long iron chains from either end of two poles laid on the wall and projecting over it, drew them up at an angle whenever any point was threatened by the engine, and then released their hold and let the beam go with its chains slack, so that it fell with a rush and snapped off the nose of the battering ram.

After this, the Peloponnesians, finding that their engines were doing nothing and that their mound was being matched by the counterwork, concluded that their present means of attack were not enough to take the city, and prepared for a circumvallation. First, however, they decided to try fire and see whether, with the help of a wind, they could burn the town, since it was not large. Indeed, they thought of every possible expedient by which the place might be reduced without the expense of a blockade. They accordingly brought up bundles of brushwood and threw them from the mound, first into the space between the mound and the wall. This soon filled up, given the number of hands at work, and they next heaped the bundles as far into the town as they could reach from the top, and then set the wood ablaze with sulphur and pitch. The result was a fire greater than any ever yet produced by human agency — though of course it could not be compared to the spontaneous fires sometimes seen when wind rubs the branches of a mountain forest together. The fire was remarkable not only for its size; at the end of so many dangers, it also came within an ace of being fatal to the Plataeans. A great part of the town became entirely inaccessible, and had a wind blown on it, as the enemy hoped, nothing could have saved them. As it was, there is also a story that heavy rain and thunder came on, by which the fire was put out and the danger averted.

Having failed in this last attempt, the Peloponnesians left a portion of their forces on the spot, dismissed the rest, and built a wall of circumvallation around the town, dividing the ground among the various cities present. A ditch was made within and without the lines, from which they got their bricks. By about the rising of Arcturus all was finished. They left enough men to garrison half the wall, the rest being manned by the Boeotians, and the army withdrew and dispersed to its several cities. The Plataeans had previously sent off their wives and children, the oldest men, and the bulk of the non-combatants to Athens, so that the number of the besieged left in the place came to four hundred of their own citizens, eighty Athenians, and a hundred and ten women to bake their bread. This was the total at the start of the siege, and there was no one else within the walls, slave or free. Such were the arrangements made for the blockade of Plataea.

That same summer, at the same time as the expedition against Plataea, the Athenians marched with two thousand heavy infantry and two hundred horse against the Chalcidians in the direction of Thrace and against the Bottiaeans, just as the corn was ripening, under the command of Xenophon, son of Euripides, and two colleagues. Arriving before Spartolus in Bottiaea, they destroyed the corn and had some hopes that the city would come over through the intrigues of a faction within. But those of the opposite party had sent to Olynthus, and a garrison of heavy infantry and other troops accordingly arrived. These came out from Spartolus and engaged the Athenians in front of the town. The Chalcidian heavy infantry, with some auxiliaries, were beaten and retreated into Spartolus, but the Chalcidian horse and light troops defeated the horse and light troops of the Athenians. The Chalcidians already had a few targeteers from Crusis, and shortly after the battle were joined by more from Olynthus. When the light troops from Spartolus saw them, emboldened by this reinforcement and by their previous success, they joined with the Chalcidian horse and the new arrivals and attacked the Athenians again. The Athenians fell back on the two divisions they had left with their baggage. Whenever the Athenians advanced, the enemy gave way, then pressed them with missiles the moment they began to withdraw. The Chalcidian horse, riding up and charging them at will, at last produced a panic among them and routed them, pursuing them a long distance. The Athenians took refuge in Potidæa, afterwards recovered their dead under truce, and returned to Athens with the remnant of their army; four hundred and thirty men and all the generals had fallen. The Chalcidians and Bottiaeans set up a trophy, took up their dead, and dispersed to their several cities.

That same summer, not long after this, the Ambraciots and Chaonians, wishing to reduce the whole of Acarnania and detach it from Athens, persuaded the Lacedaemonians to fit out a fleet from their confederacy and send a thousand heavy infantry to Acarnania. Their argument was that, if a combined movement were made by land and sea, the coastal Acarnanians would be unable to march; that the conquest of Zacynthus and Cephallenia would easily follow on the possession of Acarnania, so that the cruise round the Peloponnese would no longer be so convenient for the Athenians; and besides this, there was a hope of taking Naupactus. The Lacedaemonians accordingly sent off at once a few vessels with Cnemus, who was still high admiral, and the heavy infantry on board, and sent round orders for the rest of the fleet to be readied as quickly as possible and to sail to Leucas. The Corinthians were the most active in the business, since the Ambraciots were a colony of theirs. While the ships from Corinth, Sicyon, and the surrounding region were getting ready, and those from Leucas, Anactorium, and Ambracia, which had arrived earlier, were waiting for them at Leucas, Cnemus and his thousand heavy infantry had run into the gulf, slipping past Phormio, the commander of the Athenian squadron stationed off Naupactus, and at once began to prepare for the land expedition. The Hellenic troops with him consisted of the Ambraciots, Leucadians, and Anactorians, and the thousand Peloponnesians he had brought; the barbarian troops, of a thousand Chaonians, who, belonging to a nation that has no king, were led by Photys and Nicanor, the two members of the royal family entrusted with the chieftainship for that year. With the Chaonians came also some Thesprotians, who like them had no king, some Molossians and Atintanians led by Sabylinthus, the guardian of King Tharyps, who was still a minor, and some Paravaeans under their king Oroedus, accompanied by a thousand Orestians, subjects of King Antiochus, placed by him under the command of Oroedus. There were also a thousand Macedonians sent by Perdiccas without the knowledge of the Athenians, but they arrived too late. With this force Cnemus set out, without waiting for the fleet from Corinth. Passing through the territory of Amphilochian Argos, sacking the open village of Limnaea, they advanced to Stratus, the Acarnanian capital. Once that was taken, they were convinced, the rest of the country would soon follow.

The Acarnanians, finding themselves invaded by a large army on land and threatened by a hostile fleet from the sea, made no combined attempt at resistance, but stayed to defend their homes and sent for help to Phormio. He replied that, with a fleet about to sail from Corinth, it was impossible for him to leave Naupactus unprotected. The Peloponnesians and their allies meanwhile advanced on Stratus in three divisions, intending to encamp near it and to attempt the wall by force if they failed to take it by negotiation. The order of march was as follows: the centre was held by the Chaonians and the rest of the barbarians; the Leucadians and Anactorians and their followers held the right; and Cnemus, with the Peloponnesians and Ambraciots, held the left. The divisions were a long way apart, sometimes even out of sight of each other. The Hellenes advanced in good order, keeping a lookout until they encamped in a strong position. But the Chaonians, full of self-confidence, having the highest reputation for courage among the tribes of that part of the mainland, did not wait to occupy their camp; they rushed on with the rest of the barbarians, thinking they could take the town by assault and claim the sole glory of the enterprise. While they were coming on, the Stratians, becoming aware how things stood and thinking that the defeat of this division would seriously dishearten the Hellenes behind it, set ambushes around the town, and as soon as the Chaonians approached, engaged them at close quarters from the city and from the ambushes. A panic seized the Chaonians, great numbers of them were killed, and as soon as they were seen to give way, the rest of the barbarians turned and fled. Because of the distance by which their allies had outpaced them, neither of the Hellenic divisions knew anything of the battle; they imagined the others were simply hurrying to encamp. When, however, the fleeing barbarians broke in upon them, they opened their ranks to receive them, brought their divisions together, and stayed quiet where they were for the day. The Stratians did not offer to engage them, since the rest of the Acarnanians had not yet arrived; instead they contented themselves with slinging at them from a distance, which distressed them greatly, since no one could move without his armour. The Acarnanians seem to excel at this kind of warfare.

As soon as night fell, Cnemus quickly drew off his army to the river Anapus, about nine miles from Stratus. The next day he recovered his dead under truce, was joined there by the friendly Oeniadae, and fell back upon their city before the enemy's reinforcements arrived. From there each contingent returned home, and the Stratians set up a trophy for the battle with the barbarians.

Meanwhile the fleet from Corinth and the rest of the confederates in the Crissaean Gulf, which was supposed to cooperate with Cnemus and prevent the coastal Acarnanians from joining their countrymen in the interior, was prevented from doing so by being forced, about the time of the battle at Stratus, to fight Phormio and the twenty Athenian vessels stationed at Naupactus. As they coasted along out of the gulf, they were watched by Phormio, who wanted to attack in open sea. The Corinthians and their allies had set out for Acarnania with no intention of fighting at sea, and with vessels more like transports for carrying soldiers; besides which, they never imagined that the twenty Athenian ships would venture to engage their forty-seven. However, while they were coasting along their own shore, there were the Athenians sailing in line with them; and when they tried to cross over from Patrae in Achaea to the mainland on the other side, on their way to Acarnania, they saw them again coming out from Chalcis and the river Evenus to meet them. They slipped from their moorings during the night, but were spotted, and at last were forced to fight in mid-passage. Each state that contributed to the armament had its own general; the Corinthian commanders were Machaon, Isocrates, and Agatharchidas. The Peloponnesians arranged their vessels in as large a circle as possible without leaving an opening, prows outward and sterns inward; and they placed inside the circle all the small craft accompanying them, along with their five best sailers, who were to issue out at a moment's notice and reinforce any point threatened by the enemy.

The Athenians, in line, sailed round and round them, forcing them to contract their circle by continually brushing past and looking as though they would attack at any moment, having been previously cautioned by Phormio not to do so until he gave the signal. His hope was that the Peloponnesians would not hold their order like a force on shore, but that the ships would foul one another and the small craft would cause confusion; and if the wind blew from the gulf — which usually rose toward morning, and which was the reason he kept circling them — they would not, he was sure, hold steady for an instant. He also thought it was up to him to attack when he chose, since his ships sailed better, and that an attack timed to the coming of the wind would have the most effect. When the wind came down, the enemy's ships were now packed into a narrow space, and what with the wind and the small craft crashing against them, they at once fell into confusion. Ship fouled ship, while the crews tried to push them off with poles, and by their shouting, swearing, and struggling with one another made the captains' orders and the boatswains' calls equally inaudible; and from being unable, for lack of practice, to clear their oars in the rough water, they prevented the vessels from properly obeying the helm. At this moment Phormio gave the signal, and the Athenians attacked. They first sank one of the admirals' ships, then disabled every vessel they came up against, so that no one thought of resistance in the confusion, and they fled for Patrae and Dyme in Achaea. The Athenians gave chase and captured twelve ships, took most of the men out of them, and sailed to Molycrium; after setting up a trophy on the promontory of Rhium and dedicating a ship to Poseidon, they returned to Naupactus. As for the Peloponnesians, they at once sailed with their remaining ships along the coast from Dyme and Patrae to Cyllene, the Eleian arsenal, where Cnemus and the ships from Leucas that were to have joined them also arrived after the battle at Stratus.

The Lacedaemonians now sent three commissioners — Timocrates, Brasidas, and Lycophron — to Cnemus's fleet, with orders to prepare to engage again with better fortune, and not to be driven from the sea by a few vessels. They could not at all account for the defeat, especially as it was their first attempt at sea, and they imagined that it was not that their navy was so inferior, but that there had been misconduct somewhere — not taking into account the long experience of the Athenians compared with the little practice they had had themselves. The commissioners were therefore sent in anger. As soon as they arrived they set to work with Cnemus to order ships from the various states and to put the ones they already had into fighting order. Meanwhile Phormio sent word to Athens of their preparations and of his own victory, asking that as many ships as possible be sent to him quickly, since he was in daily expectation of a battle. Twenty were accordingly sent, but their commander was instructed to go first to Crete. For Nicias, a Cretan of Gortys who was proxenus of the Athenians, had persuaded them to sail against Cydonia, promising to bring about the reduction of that hostile town. His real wish was to oblige the Polichnitans, neighbours of the Cydonians. He accordingly went with the ships to Crete, and, accompanied by the Polichnitans, laid waste the lands of the Cydonians; and, with adverse winds and bad weather, wasted a good deal of time there.

While the Athenians were thus held up in Crete, the Peloponnesians at Cyllene got ready for battle and coasted along to Panormus in Achaea, where their land army had come to support them. Phormio also coasted along to Molycrian Rhium, and anchored outside it with the same twenty ships he had fought with before. This Rhium was friendly to the Athenians. The other, in the Peloponnese, lies opposite it; the sea between them is about three-quarters of a mile wide and forms the mouth of the Crissaean Gulf. At the Achaean Rhium, not far off Panormus where their army lay, the Peloponnesians now cast anchor with seventy-seven ships, when they saw the Athenians do the same. For six or seven days they lay opposite each other, training and preparing for the battle: one side resolved not to sail out of the Rhia into the open sea, for fear of the disaster they had already suffered there; the other not to sail into the straits, thinking it would be to the enemy's advantage to fight in the narrows. At last Cnemus and Brasidas and the rest of the Peloponnesian commanders, wanting to bring on a battle as soon as possible, before reinforcements should arrive from Athens, and noticing that most of the men were cowed by the previous defeat and had lost heart for the business, first called them together and encouraged them as follows:

“Peloponnesians, the late engagement, which may have made some of you afraid of the one now in prospect, really gives no just ground for apprehension. Preparation for it, as you know, was scant enough; and the object of our voyage was not so much to fight at sea as an expedition by land. Besides this, the chances of war were largely against us; and perhaps also inexperience had something to do with our failure in our first naval action. It was not, therefore, cowardice that produced our defeat, nor ought a determination that force has not quelled, but that still has something to say to its adversary, to lose its edge through the result of an accident. Granted that there can be a chance miscarriage, we should know that brave hearts must always be brave, and while they remain so can never plead inexperience as an excuse for misconduct. Nor are you so far behind the enemy in experience as you are ahead of him in courage; and though their skill, if accompanied by valour, would also have the presence of mind to apply in an emergency the lesson it has learned, yet a faint heart makes all skill useless in the face of danger. Fear takes away presence of mind, and without valour, skill is useless. Set your superior daring against their superior experience, and against the fear born of defeat set the fact that you were then unprepared. Remember, too, that you have the advantage of superior numbers, and of engaging off your own coast, supported by your heavy infantry; and as a rule, numbers and equipment win victory. At no point, then, is defeat likely; and as for our previous mistakes, the very fact that they happened will teach us better for the future. Steersmen and sailors, therefore, may attend with confidence to their several duties, none leaving the station assigned to him. As for ourselves, we promise to prepare for the engagement at least as well as your previous commanders, and to give no excuse for any man's misconduct. Should anyone insist on misconduct, he shall meet with the punishment he deserves, while the brave shall be honoured with the proper rewards of valour.”

The Peloponnesian commanders encouraged their men in this manner. Phormio, meanwhile, being himself not without fears for the courage of his men, and noticing that they were forming in groups among themselves and were alarmed at the odds against them, wanted to call them together and give them confidence and counsel in the present emergency. He had before this constantly told them, and had trained their minds to accept, that there was no numerical superiority they could not face; and the men themselves had long been persuaded that Athenians need never retreat before any number of Peloponnesian vessels. At the moment, however, he saw that they were dispirited by the sight before them, and wanting to refresh their confidence, he called them together and spoke as follows:

“I see, men, that you are alarmed by the number of the enemy, and so I have called you together — I do not want you to be afraid of what is not really fearful. In the first place, the Peloponnesians, already defeated, and not even themselves believing they are a match for us, have not ventured to meet us on equal terms, but have equipped this great fleet against us. Next, as for the thing they most rely on — the courage they suppose to be natural to them — their confidence here arises only from the success their experience in land service usually gives them, and which they imagine will do the same for them at sea. But this advantage will in all justice belong to us on this element, if to them on theirs. They are not superior to us in courage; each of us is more confident according to our experience in our particular department. Besides, since the Lacedaemonians use their supremacy over their allies to promote their own glory, most of these allies are being led into danger against their will — otherwise they would never, after such a decisive defeat, have ventured on a fresh engagement. You need not, therefore, be afraid of their dash. You, on the contrary, inspire a much greater and better-grounded alarm, both because of your recent victory and because they believe we would not face them unless we were about to do something worthy of so signal a success. An adversary numerically superior, like the one before us, comes into action trusting more to strength than to resolution, while a man who voluntarily confronts tremendous odds must have very great resources of his own to draw on. For these reasons the Peloponnesians fear our irrational audacity more than they would ever have feared a more proportionate force. Besides, many great armaments have before now been beaten by smaller ones through lack of skill or sometimes of courage; neither of which defects are ours. As for the battle, it shall not be, if I can help it, in the strait, nor will I sail in there at all. In a contest between a number of clumsily handled vessels and a small, fast, well-handled squadron, lack of sea room is an undoubted disadvantage. One cannot ram an enemy properly without sighting him a good way off, nor can one back off when pressed; one can neither break the line nor return on the rear, the proper tactics of a fast sailer. The naval action necessarily becomes a land one, in which numbers must decide. For all this I will provide as far as I can. Stay at your posts by your ships, and be sharp at catching the word of command, all the more so since we are observing one another from such a short distance. In action, treat order and silence as all-important — qualities useful in war generally, and in naval engagements in particular. Behave before the enemy in a manner worthy of your past exploits. The issues you fight for are great: to destroy the naval hopes of the Peloponnesians, or to bring closer to the Athenians their fears for the sea. And let me remind you once again that you have already defeated most of them, and beaten men do not face a danger twice with the same determination.”

Such was Phormio's exhortation. The Peloponnesians, finding that the Athenians did not sail into the gulf and the narrows, decided to lead them in whether they wished it or not. They put out at dawn and, forming four abreast, sailed inside the gulf in the direction of their own country, the right wing leading as they had lain at anchor. Twenty of their best sailers were placed in this wing, so that if Phormio should think their object was Naupactus and coast along to save the place, the Athenians might not be able to escape their onset by getting outside the wing, but would be cut off by these vessels. As they expected, Phormio, alarmed for the place, which at that moment was empty of its garrison, as soon as he saw them put out, reluctantly and hurriedly embarked and sailed along the shore, the Messenian land forces moving along too in support. The Peloponnesians, seeing him coasting along with his ships in single file, and now inside the gulf and close inshore, just as they wished, at one signal tacked suddenly and bore down in line at their best speed on the Athenians, hoping to cut off the whole squadron. The eleven leading vessels, however, escaped the Peloponnesian wing and its sudden movement and reached the more open water; but the rest were overtaken as they tried to run through, were driven ashore and disabled, and any of the crews who had not swum out of them were killed. Some of the ships the Peloponnesians lashed to their own and towed off empty; one they took with the men still in it; others were just being towed away when the Messenians dashed into the sea in their armour and saved them by boarding the decks and fighting from them.

Thus far the victory was with the Peloponnesians, and the Athenian fleet destroyed. Meanwhile the twenty ships in the right wing were chasing the eleven Athenian vessels that had escaped the sudden movement and reached the more open water. These, with the exception of one ship, all outsailed them and got safely into Naupactus, where they formed close inshore opposite the temple of Apollo, with their prows facing the enemy, ready to defend themselves if the Peloponnesians should sail inshore against them. After a while the Peloponnesians came up, chanting the paean for their victory as they sailed on; the single Athenian ship still remaining was being chased by a Leucadian far ahead of the rest. There happened, however, to be a merchantman lying at anchor in the roadstead, which the Athenian ship had time to sail round, and then struck the pursuing Leucadian amidships and sank her. An exploit so sudden and unexpected produced a panic among the Peloponnesians; and having fallen out of order in the excitement of victory, some of them dropped their oars and stopped their way to let the main body come up — an unsafe thing to do considering how near they were to the enemy's prows; while others ran aground in the shallows, in their ignorance of the local waters.

Elated by this incident, the Athenians at one word gave a cheer and dashed at the enemy, who, embarrassed by his mistakes and the disorder he found himself in, only stood for an instant and then fled for Panormus, from where he had put out. The Athenians, on his heels, took the six vessels nearest them, and recovered those of their own which had been disabled close inshore and taken in tow at the start of the action. They killed some of the crews and took some prisoners. On board the Leucadian which went down off the merchantman was the Lacedaemonian Timocrates, who killed himself when the ship was sunk and whose body was washed up in the harbour of Naupactus. On their return, the Athenians set up a trophy on the spot from which they had put out and turned the day, picked up the wrecks and dead on their own shore, and gave back the enemy's dead under truce. The Peloponnesians also set up a trophy as victors for the defeat they had inflicted on the ships they had disabled inshore, and dedicated the vessel they had taken at Achaean Rhium, side by side with the trophy. After this, apprehensive of the reinforcement expected from Athens, all except the Leucadians sailed into the Crissaean Gulf for Corinth. Not long after their retreat, the twenty Athenian ships that were to have joined Phormio before the battle arrived at Naupactus.

So the summer ended. Winter was now at hand. But although the fleet had been dispersed and had retired to Corinth and the Crissaean Gulf, Cnemus, Brasidas, and the other Peloponnesian captains were persuaded by the Megarians to attempt a strike on Piraeus, the port of Athens, which because of her decisive superiority at sea had naturally been left unguarded and open. The plan was as follows. The men were each to carry their oar, cushion, and rowlock thong, and, going overland from Corinth to the sea on the Athenian side, to get to Megara as quickly as they could, launch the forty vessels that happened to be in the docks at Nisaea, and sail at once to Piraeus. There was no fleet on the lookout in the harbour, and no one had the least idea that the enemy might attempt a surprise; while an open attack, it was thought, would never be deliberately ventured on, or, if it were planned, would be quickly known at Athens. Plan formed, the next step was to carry it out. Arriving by night and launching the vessels from Nisaea, they sailed — not to Piraeus, as they had originally intended, since they were afraid of the risk (besides, there was some talk of a wind having stopped them) — but to the point of Salamis that looks toward Megara, where there was a fort and a squadron of three ships to prevent anything from sailing in or out of Megara. They assaulted this fort, towed off the galleys empty, and, taking the inhabitants by surprise, began to lay waste the rest of the island.

Meanwhile fire signals were raised to alarm Athens, and a panic broke out there as severe as any during the war. The belief in the city was that the enemy had already sailed into Piraeus; in Piraeus it was thought that Salamis had been taken and that the enemy might at any moment arrive in the port — as indeed might easily have happened if their hearts had been a little firmer; certainly no wind would have stopped them. As soon as day broke, the Athenians assembled in full force, launched their ships, and embarking in haste and uproar went with the fleet to Salamis, while their soldiers mounted guard in Piraeus. The Peloponnesians, on becoming aware of the coming relief, and after overrunning most of Salamis, sailed off in haste with their plunder and captives and the three ships from Fort Budorum, back to Nisaea. The state of their ships was also a worry, since it was a long while since they had been launched and they were no longer water-tight. Arrived at Megara, they returned on foot to Corinth. The Athenians, finding them no longer at Salamis, sailed back themselves, and after this made arrangements to guard Piraeus more diligently in future, by closing the harbours and by other suitable precautions.

About the same time, at the beginning of this winter, Sitalces, son of Teres, the Odrysian king of Thrace, made an expedition against Perdiccas, son of Alexander, king of Macedonia, and against the Chalcidians in the neighbourhood of Thrace. His object was to enforce one promise and fulfil another. On the one hand, Perdiccas, when hard pressed at the start of the war, had made him a promise on condition that Sitalces would reconcile the Athenians to him and not try to restore his brother and enemy, the pretender Philip; but Perdiccas had not offered to fulfil his side of the deal. On the other hand, Sitalces himself, on entering into alliance with the Athenians, had agreed to put an end to the Chalcidian war in Thrace. These were the two aims of his invasion. He brought with him Amyntas, son of Philip, whom he intended for the throne of Macedonia; some Athenian envoys then at his court on this business; and Hagnon as general — for the Athenians were to join him against the Chalcidians with a fleet and as many soldiers as they could muster.

Beginning with the Odrysians, he first called out the Thracian tribes subject to him between Mount Haemus, Mount Rhodope, the Euxine, and the Hellespont; next the Getae beyond Haemus, and the other hordes settled south of the Danube in the neighbourhood of the Euxine, who, like the Getae, border on the Scythians and are armed the same way, being all mounted archers. Besides these he summoned many of the independent hill Thracian swordsmen, called Dii and mostly inhabiting Mount Rhodope, some of whom came as mercenaries, others as volunteers. He also summoned the Agrianes and Laeaeans and the rest of the Paeonian tribes in his empire, at the edge of which these lay, extending up to the Laeaean Paeonians and the river Strymon, which flows from Mount Scombrus through the country of the Agrianes and Laeaeans. There the empire of Sitalces ends and the territory of the independent Paeonians begins. Bordering on the Triballi, also independent, were the Treres and Tilataeans, who live north of Mount Scombrus and extend westward as far as the river Oskius. This river rises in the same mountains as the Nestus and the Hebrus — a wild and extensive range connected with Rhodope.

The empire of the Odrysians extended along the seaboard from Abdera to the mouth of the Danube on the Euxine. Sailing along this coast by the shortest route takes a merchantman four days and four nights with a wind astern the whole way; by land, an active man, going by the shortest road, can get from Abdera to the Danube in eleven days. Such was the length of its coastline. Inland, from Byzantium to the Laeaeans and the Strymon — the farthest extent of the empire into the interior — is a journey of thirteen days for an active man. The tribute from all the barbarian districts and Hellenic cities, taking what came in under Seuthes, the successor of Sitalces, who raised it to its greatest height, amounted to about four hundred talents in gold and silver. There were also presents in gold and silver to no smaller a sum, besides cloth, plain and embroidered, and other articles, made not only for the king but also for the Odrysian lords and nobles. The custom established here was the opposite of that in the Persian kingdom: it was a custom of taking rather than giving, more disgrace being attached to refusing to give when asked than to asking and being refused. Although this prevailed elsewhere in Thrace, it was practised most extensively among the powerful Odrysians, since nothing could be done without a present. It was thus a very powerful kingdom, surpassing in revenue and general prosperity all the kingdoms of Europe between the Ionian Gulf and the Euxine, and in numbers and military resources coming clearly next to the Scythians, with whom indeed no people in Europe can be compared — there is not even any nation in Asia that singly is a match for them when they are united, though of course they are not on a level with other races in general intelligence and the arts of civilized life.

It was the master of this empire who now prepared to take the field. When everything was ready, he set out on his march for Macedonia, first through his own dominions, then over the desolate range of Cercine, which divides the Sintians and Paeonians, crossing by a road he had cut through by felling the timber on a previous campaign against the Paeonians. Passing over these mountains, with the Paeonians on his right and the Sintians and Maedians on the left, he finally arrived at Doberus in Paeonia, losing none of his army on the march, except perhaps to sickness, but receiving some additions, since many of the independent Thracians volunteered to join him in hope of plunder. The whole is said to have come to a grand total of a hundred and fifty thousand. Most of this was infantry, though about a third was cavalry, supplied chiefly by the Odrysians themselves and next by the Getae. The most warlike of the infantry were the independent swordsmen who came down from Rhodope; the rest of the mixed multitude that followed him was formidable mainly in numbers.

Assembling at Doberus, they prepared to descend from the heights into Lower Macedonia, where the dominions of Perdiccas lay. The Lyncestae, Elimiots, and other tribes farther inland, though Macedonians by blood, and allies and dependants of their kindred, still have their own separate governments. The country on the seacoast, now called Macedonia, was first acquired by Alexander, the father of Perdiccas, and his ancestors, originally Temenids from Argos. This was achieved by the expulsion of the Pierians from Pieria, who afterwards settled at Phagres and other places under Mount Pangaeus, beyond the Strymon (indeed, the country between Pangaeus and the sea is still called the Pierian Gulf); by the expulsion of the Bottiaeans, now neighbours of the Chalcidians, from Bottia; by the acquisition in Paeonia of a narrow strip along the river Axius extending to Pella and the sea; and by the addition of the district of Mygdonia, between the Axius and the Strymon, after the expulsion of the Edonians. From Eordia they also drove out the Eordians, most of whom perished, though a few still live around Physca; and the Almopians from Almopia. These Macedonians also conquered places belonging to the other tribes, which are still theirs — Anthemus, Crestonia, Bisaltia, and much of Macedonia proper. The whole is now called Macedonia, and at the time of the invasion of Sitalces, Perdiccas, son of Alexander, was the reigning king.

These Macedonians, unable to take the field against so numerous an invader, shut themselves up in such strongholds and forts as the country possessed. There were not many of these — most of those now found in the country having been built later by Archelaus, son of Perdiccas, on his accession, who also cut straight roads and otherwise put the kingdom on a better footing as regards horses, heavy infantry, and other military equipment than all the eight kings before him had done. Advancing from Doberus, the Thracian host first invaded what had once been Philip's government, and took Idomene by assault, and Gortynia, Atalanta, and some other places by negotiation — these last coming over out of attachment to Philip's son, Amyntas, then with Sitalces. He laid siege to Europus, but failed to take it; he then advanced into the rest of Macedonia, to the left of Pella and Cyrrhus, but did not press beyond this into Bottiaea and Pieria, staying instead to lay waste Mygdonia, Crestonia, and Anthemus.

The Macedonians never even thought of meeting him with infantry; instead, the Thracian host was attacked, as opportunity offered, by small detachments of their horse, which had been reinforced from their allies in the interior. Armed with cuirasses and excellent horsemen, wherever these charged they overthrew all before them, but they ran considerable risk in entangling themselves in the enemy's masses, and so finally gave up the attempt, judging themselves not strong enough to venture against such superior numbers.

Meanwhile Sitalces opened negotiations with Perdiccas on the objects of his expedition. Finding that the Athenians, not believing he would come, did not appear with their fleet (though they sent presents and envoys), he detached a large part of his army against the Chalcidians and Bottiaeans, shut them inside their walls, and laid waste their country. While he remained in these parts, the peoples farther south — the Thessalians, Magnetes, the other tribes subject to the Thessalians, and the Hellenes as far as Thermopylae — all feared that the army might advance against them, and made their preparations accordingly. These fears were shared by the Thracians beyond the Strymon to the north, who inhabited the plains — the Panaeans, Odomanti, Droi, and Dersaeans, all of whom are independent. It was even a matter of conversation among the Hellenes who were enemies of Athens whether he might not be invited by his ally to advance against them too. Meanwhile he held Chalcidice, Bottice, and Macedonia, and was ravaging them all; but finding that he was succeeding in none of the objects of his invasion, and that his army was without provisions and suffering from the severity of the weather, he listened to the advice of Seuthes, son of Spardacus, his nephew and highest officer, and decided to retreat without delay. Seuthes had been secretly won over by Perdiccas, who promised him his sister in marriage with a rich dowry. Following this advice, and after a stay of thirty days in all, eight of which were spent in Chalcidice, he withdrew home as quickly as he could; and Perdiccas afterwards gave his sister Stratonice to Seuthes as he had promised. Such was the history of the expedition of Sitalces.

In the course of this winter, after the dispersion of the Peloponnesian fleet, the Athenians in Naupactus, under Phormio, coasted along to Astacus and disembarked, and marched into the interior of Acarnania with four hundred Athenian heavy infantry and four hundred Messenians. After expelling some suspected persons from Stratus, Coronta, and other places, and restoring Cynes, son of Theolytus, to Coronta, they returned to their ships, deciding it was impossible in the winter season to march against Oeniadae, a place that, unlike the rest of Acarnania, had always been hostile to them. For the river Achelous flows from Mount Pindus through Dolopia and the country of the Agraeans and Amphilochians and the plain of Acarnania, past the town of Stratus in its upper course, and forms lakes where it falls into the sea around Oeniadae, making the area impracticable for an army in winter because of the water. Opposite Oeniadae lie most of the islands called the Echinades, so close to the mouths of the Achelous that that powerful stream is constantly piling up deposits against them, and has already joined some of the islands to the mainland, and seems likely before long to do the same with the rest. The current is strong, deep, and muddy, and the islands lie so thick together that they trap the alluvial deposit and prevent it from dispersing — they lie not in one line but irregularly, leaving no direct channel for the water into the open sea. The islands in question are uninhabited and not of any great size. There is also a story that Alcmaeon, son of Amphiaraus, during his wanderings after the murder of his mother, was told by Apollo to settle on this spot, through an oracle which suggested that he would have no release from his terrors until he found a country to live in that had not been seen by the sun, nor existed as land, at the time he killed his mother — for all other ground was polluted to him. Perplexed at this, the story goes on, he at last noticed this deposit of the Achelous, and judged that a place sufficient to support life on might have been thrown up during the long interval that had passed since his mother's death and the beginning of his wanderings. So he settled in the district around Oeniadae, founded a dominion, and gave the country its name from his son Acarnan. Such is the story we have received concerning Alcmaeon.

The Athenians and Phormio, putting back from Acarnania and arriving at Naupactus, sailed home to Athens in the spring, taking with them the ships they had captured and such of the prisoners taken in the late actions as were freemen, who were exchanged man for man. And so ended this winter, and the third year of this war, of which Thucydides was the historian.
